summary: US President Donald Trump delayed planned 50% tariffs on Canadian goods for three days, stating that a trade deal is close pending document finalization. The threatened levies would have affected nearly $20bn of Canadian imports, including wine, dairy, cement, clothing, and hockey equipment. Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney confirmed substantial progress has been made, though important work remains.
key_points: President Trump paused scheduled 50% tariffs on Canadian goods for a three-day period.
The delay was announced as the US and Canada work to finalize a pending trade agreement.
A finalized trade deal could potentially revive the Keystone XL pipeline project.
Key discussion points have included US tariffs on autos and Canadian provincial bans on American liquor sales.

title: Iran-US war live: Trump declares Strait of Hormuz as US territory with bizarre map
author: Dan Haygarth; Daniel Haygarth; Maira Butt; Sam Rkaina
content:
President Donald Trump has declared the Strait of Hormuz as US territory in a new post on Truth Social.
Sharing a crude map of the region with a large blue circle over Hormuz, the picture declared the vital shipping route as “NEW US territory”.
“The Naval Blockade remains in full force and effect,” he continued. “The Hormuz Strait is open and operating. All water mines have been removed or detonated.”
However, data shared by Kpler with The Independent shows that only ten vessels passed through on Monday, compared to 130 to 140 before the outbreak of war.
Trump earlier confirmed that there are “no talks or conversations going on, or scheduled” with the Islamic Republic of Iran.
Iran had earlier said the shipping route is to remain closed until the US meet the conditions agreed in an interim deal, according to Iran’s top negotiator Mohammed Bagher Ghalibaf in comments shared by state media.
Conditions include lifting a marine blockade and sanctions as well as freeing Iran’s frozen assets.
Comment - Donald Trump has found exciting new ways to embarrass America – can this one man stop him?
![](https://static.independent.co.uk/2026/08/18/10/56/TrumpOsoff-split-9a4aedac.jpeg?trim=0,0,0,0&width=1200&height=800&crop=1200:800)
Israeli airstrikes hit Syrian airbase, drawing Turkish condemnation
Israel bombed an airbase in Syria on Tuesday, Syrian state media said, carrying out what appeared to be its first strike on Syrian government assets since March and drawing condemnation from Turkey and criticism from a US envoy who called it an "unnecessary escalation".
Syria's state-run Ekhbariya, citing a military source, said Israel carried out eight airstrikes on the runway and storage facilities at the Abu al-Duhur base, while a separate military source and a civilian who lives near the base said there were no casualties.
The Israeli military declined to comment on the strikes, while the Syrian defence ministry did not respond.
"We are deeply concerned that the confirmed Israeli airstrikes on Abu al-Duhur Airbase constitute an unnecessary escalation that does not advance regional stability," ambassador Tom Barrack, the US special presidential envoy for Syria and Iraq, said on X.
"The United States continues to believe that restraint and engagement offer the more constructive course. We encourage all parties to prioritize logical discourse over further military incidents," he added.
Syrian foreign minister Assad al-Shibani called for the attacks to stop, saying Israel should recalculate its position toward Syria because it faced not only Damascus, but also its allies through its strikes.
Trump is threatening to bomb Oman, but why?
Explainer by the Associated Press
Oman has played a relatively low-profile role since the Iran war began, including as a mediator.
But its geography has thrust it into the uncomfortable position of negotiating with Tehran over management of the strait while facing Trump's threats.
Trump this week told Fox News reporter Trey Yingst that the U.S. would bomb Oman if it "gets in the way," using an expletive for emphasis. It's not the first such threat he's made. Oman has not commented.
Trump is not happy about the emerging Oman-Iran deal
Trump threatened Oman because he's not happy that it's close to a deal with Iran over the strait, two regional officials said Tuesday.
US-Iran negotiations have dried up.
This week ended the 60-day period that launched when the US and Iran signed an interim agreement. It had been meant to open the way for more detailed talks.
There's no sign of it being extended. Trump now says there are no planned talks with Iran.
So the only confirmed discussions happening now are between Iran and Oman about shipping on the strait.
These have been going on for weeks. Oman hasn't said much about them publicly.
Tehran says they're finalising a joint statement.
Trump has made plenty of threats against Iran. Now he's venting his frustration at Oman, too.
Now Oman is in discussions that appear to be driven by Iran, which has described the talks as aiming to "develop mechanisms to ensure safe navigation through the Strait of Hormuz while respecting the sovereign rights and sovereignty of both coastal states, as well as Iran's security and national interests."
The mechanisms might include fees.
How the Iran war is forcing families to choose between schooling and survival
Sou Sreynich dreams of becoming a teacher. But she knows she's far behind.
The 13-year-old first entered a classroom at 10, an age when most Cambodian children already have been in school for years. Her mother waited until she was old enough to swim, fearing the boat to school could capsize — a decision familiar to many parents on Cambodia's Tonle Sap, the largest freshwater lake in Southeast Asia.
Now, the price of gasoline has spiked because of the Iran war, an additional burden. Unlike outright school closures during Covid-19, the Iran war’s impact on education is less visible.
From America’s ‘oldest ally’ in the Middle East to a bombing target: Trump is trying to wreck the US-Omani relationship
On Monday, President Donald Trump made yet another unprecedented and violent threat against a country in the Middle East.
But this time the target of his ire was unexpected. Oman, an American ally for almost 200 years, would be bombed “to s***” if it interfered with a potential US-Iran peace deal, Trump told a FOX News reporter.
It was not the first time that Trump had threatened Oman, previously warning the country in May to “behave” or face potential military action.
Throughout the US-Israeli war in Iran, Muscat has endured retaliatory strikes across its ports and energy infrastructure but has nevertheless taken part in negotiations towards a resolution.
Watch: Netanyahu puts NYC mayor Mamdani alongside Iran’s Ayatollah on enemies list
UAE says Iran launched two missiles at it
The UAE's defence ministry said on Tuesday that it detected two ballistic missiles launched from Iran against the Gulf country. It said one fell inside territorial waters, while another fell outside, and stressed the UAE's readiness to deal with any threats.
There was no immediate comment from Iran.
Earlier on Tuesday, the UAE's interior ministry sent a phone alert stating that the situation was safe and people should resume normal activities after an earlier alert warning of a missile threat.
US oil reserves are so low amid Trump’s Iran war the caverns holding them could be damaged
America’s emergency oil stockpile has dropped to its lowest level in 40 years, with experts warning that ongoing withdrawals for the war with Iran could permanently damage the underground caverns holding the crude.
The warnings arrive as American drivers face unprecedented gas prices for late summer. Today’s AAA National Average for a gallon of regular gasoline sits at $4.07, marking the highest levels on record for mid-August.
Concerns over the physical limits of the Strategic Petroleum Reserve center on the unique geology of its storage network. The crude is held within 60 salt caverns thousands of feet below ground at four sites across Texas and Louisiana.
To extract crude, operators pump fresh water into the bottom of a cavern to force oil up to pipeline intakes. However, petroleum engineering professor Siddharth Misra of Texas A&M University told CNBC that repeated rapid drawdowns wash away salt walls.
![](https://static.independent.co.uk/2026/08/15/20/14/GettyImages-1434807937.jpeg?trim=171,0,241,0&width=1200&height=800&crop=1200:800)
Trump's crude Hormuz map includes parts of Iran
Donald Trump has posted a map identifying the Strait of Hormuz as “new U.S. territory”, echoing a threat he made last week under the continued pressure of the key waterway’s contested nature.
In a captionless post on Truth Social, the president circled the strait and labeled it “new U.S. territory.”
U.S. forces, however, have been unable to guarantee safe passage for ships through the strait thus far and the circle depicted on Trump’s map actually includes quite a bit of Iranian land on the northern borders of the strait.
That would imply a partial U.S. occupation of Iranian soil.
![Trump posted the map alongside his ‘declaration’ on Truth Social](https://static.independent.co.uk/2026/08/18/12/06/Trump-Hormuz-Map-Comp.png)
How a vague clause in Trump’s peace deal led to anarchy in the Strait of Hormuz
Both sides blame the other for violations of a ceasefire agreement.
The Strait of Hormuz is made up of two shipping corridors. One is a southern passage that runs along the Omani coast, which was traditionally used for inbound ships.
The second lane, generally for outbound vessels, runs along the Iranian coast. Throughout the conflict, the corridors have been used for both inbound and outbound commercial traffic.
In the days leading up to Iran’s attacks this week, tensions had been mounting as commercial traffic appeared to increase through the route along the Omani coast.
Iran said that any ships not using its approved route would face an “immediate and powerful response” and the IRGC has used various techniques, including small boats “swarming” commercial vessels.
![](https://static.independent.co.uk/2026/07/10/14/2026-07-10T130543Z_1345548046_RC25AMATSFKG_RTRMADP_3_IRAN-CRISIS-SHIPPING-UN.JPG?trim=0,429,0,429&width=1200&height=800&crop=1200:800)
summary: President Donald Trump declared the Strait of Hormuz as U.S. territory on social media using a crude map, while maintaining that a naval blockade is in effect. Meanwhile, tensions escalate as the UAE reports two ballistic missiles launched from Iran, and Israel conducts airstrikes on a Syrian airbase. Additionally, U.S. emergency oil reserves have dropped to a 40-year low due to the conflict, and Trump has threatened American ally Oman over its ongoing negotiations with Iran regarding shipping lanes.
key_points: President Trump posted a map on Truth Social declaring the Strait of Hormuz as new U.S. territory.
The UAE defense ministry reported that two ballistic missiles were launched from Iran toward the country.
Israel carried out airstrikes on the Abu al-Duhur airbase in Syria, drawing international criticism.
U.S. strategic petroleum reserves have fallen to their lowest level in 40 years, raising concerns over cavern stability and record-high gas prices.
Trump threatened military action against Oman due to its ongoing negotiations with Iran regarding the Strait of Hormuz.

title: Earthquake rocks Spain's historic Granada, injuring three
author: Jaroslav Lukiv
content:
Watch: Terrified pets and crushed cars as earthquake shakes Granada
- Published
At least three people have been lightly injured and a number of buildings damaged after an earthquake rocked southern Spain.
The epicentre of the magnitude 4.8 tremor on Tuesday morning was about 10km (six miles) south of the historic city of Granada, the country's National Geographic Institute (IGN) said.
Many local residents were seen rushing out of their homes into the streets, fearing strong aftershocks. A number of vehicles were damaged by falling debris. Some museums, administrative buildings and sports centres have been forced to close.
The IGN said it was the latest in a series of very shallow tremors in the area that started last Friday and were widely felt.
![A policeman stands at a cordoned off street near damaged vehicles following an earthquake in Granada, southern Spain. Photo: 18 August 2026](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1024/cpsprodpb/831b/live/65230d80-9b24-11f1-a291-b542ee92de7c.jpg)
A number of vehicles were damaged by falling debris in Tuesday's earthquake
The tremor struck at 10:37 local time (08:37 GMT) near the town of AlhendÃn, the IGN said. It was recorded at the depth of under 10km.
Alfonso Malpica said he felt his ground floor flat in Granada shaking, telling El PaÃs newspaper that the quake was "stronger than the ones that happen from time to time, the ones we're used to".
"Everything came crashing down. It was terrifying," Cristina Ruiz Lopez, a lab worker who was at a supermarket in Granada, was quoted as saying by the AFP news agency.
Granada's famous Alhambra palace - a Unesco World Heritage Site of medieval Islamic architecture - "will remain closed this afternoon", the site administrators said.
The palace is visited every year by millions of tourists from around the world.
Meanwhile, Granada's metro network said it was reducing the speed of its trains to 30km/h (19mph) for "safety reasons" and warned that this may cause delays.
summary: An earthquake with a magnitude of 4.8 struck southern Spain near Granada, resulting in three light injuries and building damage. Residents fled to the streets as falling debris damaged vehicles and forced the closure of museums, administrative buildings, and sports centres, including the famous Alhambra palace. The tremor was part of a series of shallow earthquakes that began the previous Friday in the area.
key_points: A 4.8 magnitude earthquake hit southern Spain near Granada on Tuesday morning.
At least three people sustained light injuries and several vehicles were damaged by falling debris.
The historic Alhambra palace and other public buildings were temporarily closed.
The tremor was the latest in a series of shallow earthquakes in the region that began on Friday.

title: Peruvian Lawyer Shot Dead at Her Table as Friends Look On
author: Adriana Guerrero
content:
![Helenn Giulianna Silva Padilla](https://s.yimg.com/lo/mysterio/api/70b2ab2783bea4a6468dce5a78c2a496de987b56fb4be8d2f81e4b6f227066b2/lightyear_networkapi/resizefill_w976%3Bquality_80%3Bformat_webp/https%3A%2F%2Fmedia.zenfs.com%2Fen%2Fwhere_is_the_buzz_814%2F7793a63dc0a1db340541f442fc9f4157.jpg)
- Peruvian lawyer Helenn Giulianna Silva Padilla was fatally shot in the head by a masked gunman while sitting at a roadside restaurant with three friends in northern Peru.
Peruvian lawyer Helenn Giulianna Silva Padilla died at the age of 44 due to gunshots fired at her by a masked person while she was sitting with three of her friends at a roadside restaurant in northern Peru.
According to witnesses, a dark-helmeted gunman approached the metal grating around the Pikeitos roadside restaurant in the San Martín de Porres location, San José district of Pacasmayo province, at 5:55 pm on August 15th, where the woman was with three other people. He started to shoot; one round hit her in the head.
Fortunately, no one else was injured, and they took her to Tomás Lafora Hospital in the neighboring town of Guadalupe. Doctors stated that she passed away there. She had two children.
Two persons on a motorbike appeared before the murder, but unfortunately, the murderer managed to escape on that vehicle together with the second man who came earlier. In addition, it is said that the gunman was wearing a gray sweatshirt, a dark helmet, and blue cotton trousers. Local police have cordoned off the area and collected evidence. Depincri, the Pacasmayo Criminal Investigations Division, is handling the case.
Gen. Ricardo Espinoza Cuestas, chief of the La Libertad police region, noted in an interview with Diario Correo that a working hypothesis says that a man who was once her client, but was unsatisfied with the results of the case she handled and demanded money back, was threatening her. However, the information has not yet been proven.
Furthermore, authorities claim that at the moment no one can confirm that the murder had anything to do with her profession or whether she had any threats before. Thus, they are considering all possibilities.
According to a Trome report, investigators think the suspect likely followed her. They will question the three people she was sitting with and review her recent case files, phone calls, and messages. One of the recent cases she conducted was the protection of a young man who lost his left leg after a crash with a car in May 2024, where three policemen were involved.
Surveillance cameras also captured the shooting, which spread rapidly on social media in Peru.
At this point, the La Libertad bar association issued its condolences because of the death of their member. Notably, La Libertad is a coastal region where extortion and contract killings have become more frequent lately; 132 killings have occurred there since the beginning of the year, including seven deaths in Pacasmayo province.
The post Peruvian Lawyer Shot Dead at Her Table as Friends Look On appeared first on Where Is The Buzz | Breaking News, Entertainment, Exclusive Interviews & Morero.
summary: Peruvian lawyer Helenn Giulianna Silva Padilla was shot and killed in the head by a masked gunman while dining at a roadside restaurant in northern Peru with three friends. She was taken to a nearby hospital where she was pronounced dead. Local police and the Pacasmayo Criminal Investigations Division are investigating the incident and considering multiple motives, including a potential threat from a dissatisfied former client.
key_points: Peruvian lawyer Helenn Giulianna Silva Padilla, 44, was fatally shot by a masked gunman on August 15th.
The shooting took place at the Pikeitos roadside restaurant in the San José district of Pacasmayo province.
The suspect escaped on a motorbike with an accomplice who had appeared prior to the murder.
Investigators are examining her recent case files, phone records, and surveillance footage, while exploring all possible motives.
La Libertad police noted a recent increase in extortion and contract killings in the region.

title: Disney and ABC sue Trump's media regulator to stop early licence renewal
author: Brandon Drenon; Bernd Debusmann Jr; White House reporter
content:
![An office building for KGO-TV, ABCâs channel 7 news affiliate, is seen on June  in San Francisco, California](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/608/cpsprodpb/32bd/live/f9b07010-9b1e-11f1-afea-3b9b9f2d3a59.jpg)
- Published
Disney and ABC have filed a lawsuit to stop the Trump administration from launching an early licence renewal process, arguing that the network is being unfairly targeted over its editorial content.
"Government censorship is deeply un-American," the lawsuit says. "This case concerns the Administration's sustained effort to do just that."
The lawsuit says the Federal Communication Commission - the government's media regulator - is being pressured to renew broadcast licences years early. It alleges the push stems from complaints from, and under the direction of, President Donald Trump.
FCC chairman Brendan Carr has said that the renewal requests were focused on "public interest", not retaliation.
"If broadcasters don't like that, that's okay," Carr told CNBC in July.
"They can become a cable channel, they can become a podcast, they can stream online. But if you want to uniquely be on the public's airwaves, you have to comply with those obligations."
The BBC has contacted the FCC for comment.
Disney and its eight owned-and-operated TV stations are plaintiffs in the lawsuit filed on Tuesday against FCC and its chairman.
The FCC ordered licence renewals for the Disney-owned ABC stations in April.
Disney previously had been under investigation for its alleged diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI) practices and for ABC's daytime talk show, The View.
But the notice for early renewal of licence from the FCC came a day after ABC's late-night host Jimmy Kimmel made a joke about first lady Melania Trump.
In the lawsuit, Disney calls the order by the FCC "unprecedented", saying that before then the commission had not called for early renewal in over 50 years.
"Acting through the Federal Communications Commission, the Administration has waged a retaliatory campaign against ABC for a single reason: it disapproves of what ABC broadcasts," the lawsuit says.
It cites Trump's own social media posts as evidence, including one in which Trump complained about ABC's coverage of him being "almost 100% negative".
In the same social media post, Trump also questioned whether their broadcast licences should "be terminated", and answered his own question: "I say, Yes!".
The FCC gave ABC and Disney 30 days to file applications, which, according to plaintiffs in the lawsuit, "ordinarily take months to prepare".
The lawsuit also notes that the FCC has never demanded early renewal applications from a group of stations commonly owned by a single broadcast network.
ABC and Disney have requested a "speedy hearing" from the court and a temporary restraining order.
![Brendan Carr with President Trump at an event (File picture)](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/830/cpsprodpb/a8c2/live/811b0bb0-9b23-11f1-9a2c-6d6ac3827d20.jpg)
Brendan Carr with President Trump (File picture)
Carr - who President Trump once hailed as a "warrior for free speech" - has long found himself at the centre of the administration's increasingly combative relationship with the media.
Even before assuming his position in January last year after years on the commission, Carr made clear that he would take an expansive view of his power.
ABC in particular has repeatedly drawn Carr's ire.
In September 2025, he openly threatened to take action against media companies that did not push back against comedian Jimmy Kimmel after he made remarks about the murder of conservative activist and Trump ally, Charlie Kirk.
"We can do this the easy way or the hard way," Carr told conservative podcaster Benny Johnson. "These companies can find a way to change conduct and take action, frankly, on Kimmel, or you know there's going to be additional work for the FCC ahead."
Under pressure from Carr, Disney pulled Kimmel off air.
But he was quickly returned to his role after widespread public backlash over alleged free speech violations, including from Republican Senator Ted Cruz.
Earlier, Trump successfully sued ABC News and George Stephanopoulos for defamation after the TV anchor said that the president had been found "liable for rape" in the E Jean Carroll case, rather than sexual abuse and defamation.
ABC settled the case and agreed to pay $15m for his presidential foundation and museum, plus $1m in legal fees.
- ![Jimmy Kimmel in a tuxedo holding up an Emmy Award](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/3840/cpsprodpb/43ff/live/87f486d0-95a4-11f0-816e-1bf65adb95d3.jpg)
  - Published28 April
 ![Jimmy Kimmel in a tuxedo](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1024/cpsprodpb/e841/live/16698870-4347-11f1-bd52-e755d604ece4.jpg)
  - Published20 September 2025
 ![US Senator Ted Cruz raises his left hand in front of him as he's seated behind a small microphone while speaking. He wears a blue suit and light blue shirt and tie.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1024/cpsprodpb/7a4e/live/53756e40-95a6-11f0-9c74-3fb96b77a166.jpg)
summary: Disney and ABC have filed a lawsuit against the FCC and its chairman to halt an unprecedented early broadcast licence renewal process. The legal action alleges that the Trump administration is retaliating against the network over its editorial content and comedy jokes. FCC Chairman Brendan Carr maintains that the renewal requests focus on public interest obligations rather than retaliation.
key_points: Disney and ABC filed a lawsuit to stop the FCC from enforcing an early broadcast licence renewal process.
The lawsuit claims the administration is retaliating against ABC over its editorial content and social media complaints by Donald Trump.
FCC Chairman Brendan Carr defended the move, stating it is based on public interest obligations rather than retaliation.
The FCC ordered Disney-owned ABC stations to apply for early renewal within 30 days, a demand plaintiffs say has not been made in over 50 years.

title: ABC sues Trump’s media regulator over demand for TV license renewals
author: Jeremy Barr
content:
ABC has sued the Federal Communications Commission (FCC), arguing that it is being retaliated against for content-based reasons in a move it warns threatens the independence of the press.
The network filed the lawsuit on Tuesday after being forced to apply early to renew its license to broadcast on the eight local television stations it owns. It is waiting to hear whether the Brendan Carr-led FCC approves its renewal requests, or, more likely, holds a hearing on their merits.
Late last month, a group of prominent former FCC officials, including key staffers and commissioners appointed by both Democratic and Republican presidents, issued a warning – in a filing – that the agency is trying to send a “chilling message” to broadcasters after forcing ABC to apply early.
Conservative organizations, including the Center for American Rights and the Media Research Center, filed petitions urging the FCC to deny the renewals, arguing that the network’s journalism is politically biased. ABC also still faces an FCC investigation over the daytime talkshow The View for a potential violation of equal time rules, an inquiry that remains open.
“Acting through the Federal Communications Commission, the Administration has waged a retaliatory campaign against ABC for a single reason: it disapproves of what ABC broadcasts,” the network said in the suit, filed on behalf of its eight local stations in district court for the District of Columbia.
“That campaign began in this Administration’s earliest days and has only intensified since. Again and again, the Administration has attacked ABC’s speech – the stories its journalists report and the viewpoints its network programs air. Over time, those attacks have escalated into express demands that ABC be stripped of its broadcast licenses because of its speech.”
The lawsuit makes clear that ABC does not expect the FCC to renew its licenses, posing an existential threat to the network.
“The Commission is poised to make good on its threat any day now: the public comment period on the renewal applications has closed, and the Commission may, at any moment, issue an unprecedented Hearing Designation Order for all eight Stations, which would kick off a formal agency adjudication to determine the fate of ABC’s licenses.”
The network said that any adjudication process over its licenses would be a “charade”, particularly because the agency cannot, by statute, grant license renewals several years early.
“The Commission cannot lawfully grant renewal this early in the license terms – the only outcomes on the table are adverse to Plaintiffs,” the network said in the lawsuit, expressing concern that the FCC would either “prolong” the process, “miring ABC in years of costly litigation”, or deny it altogether.
“In either scenario, the Administration accomplishes its goal of eliminating a perceived media critic: either it gets Plaintiffs to fall in line, or it silences them if they refuse,” the plaintiffs argued.
ABC’s lawyers argued that, if left unchecked, the Trump administration would have the ability to retaliate against any media company they dislike for editorial and political purposes. “If the Administration gets its way, the message to every media company in the country will be unmistakable: tell only the stories the Administration deems favorable, or face the coercive machinery of the federal government,” they wrote. “In such a world, the press could in no way be described as free.”
The network asked the court to stop the FCC from taking any actions against it or threatening any actions against it.
The Guardian has approached ABC for comment on the lawsuit.
An FCC spokesperson said: “All broadcasters have a legal obligation to operate in the public interest—even Disney. The FCC has been examining claims that Disney engaged in illegal DEI discrimination for over a year. Disney is obviously very concerned about the FCC’s proceeding, as evidenced by their ongoing campaign of disinformation as well as their decision to ask a court to stop the FCC from further pursuing matters. The FCC will continue to follow the facts and law wherever they lead.”
Gigi Sohn, who served as counselor to the chairman of the FCC during Barack Obama’s administration, said the lawsuit was a major step in the effort to fight back against the administration’s regulatory overreaches.
“For months, the FCC has waged a campaign of censorship and control against Disney’s ABC stations, using the threat of broadcast license revocations to punish a company for speech this administration doesn’t like. I have long called on companies to push back against this kind of government intimidation, and I’m glad Disney has shown courage and stepped up. This should be a welcome sign for every broadcaster who has felt the weight of this overreaching government pressure in silence,” she said.
“I am hopeful that this will mark the beginning of the end of this administration’s disregard for the Constitution and the law, and that the coming months will bring the costly legal defeat this agency has been asking for since it started down this path.”
summary: ABC has filed a lawsuit against the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) in the US district court for the District of Columbia, accusing the agency of retaliating against its content and threatening press independence. The network was forced to apply early to renew licenses for its eight local television stations following petitions from conservative groups and ongoing investigations. ABC argues that the FCC's actions are designed to punish the network for its journalism and political viewpoints.
key_points: ABC sued the FCC after being forced to submit early broadcast license renewals for its eight local TV stations.
The network alleges the administration is waging a retaliatory campaign to punish ABC for its broadcast content and journalism.
Conservative organizations previously filed petitions urging the FCC to deny the renewals due to alleged political bias.
An FCC spokesperson stated the agency is examining claims that Disney engaged in illegal DEI discrimination and must operate in the public interest.
ABC's lawsuit warns that the administration's actions threaten the independence of a free press nationwide.

title: Kildare: Officers told not to pursue car on motorway
author: Chloe Gibson
content:
Officers told not to pursue car on wrong side of motorway, says police body
![PA Media A shot of a car crash site showing a section of closed motorway with many emergency service vehicles on the road and debris from the crash.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/news/480/cpsprodpb/a34b/live/3d8de100-99fd-11f1-a7ab-8b30adf0800a.jpg.webp) PA Media
Gardaí (Irish police) were instructed to disengage from pursuing a car as it drove in the wrong direction on a motorway before a fatal crash, the Garda Representative Association has said.
Five teenagers were killed in the head-on crash on the M9 in County Kildare on Sunday morning.
Two women are in a critical condition, while another woman and a seven-year-old boy are in a serious condition.
Assistant General Secretary of the Garda Representative Association (GRA), Tara McManus, told the BBC that garda roads policing officers "do not have pursuit training".
She said officers involved in the Kildare incident were given a command to "disengage" with the car after it took "evasive action".
The crash happened on the M9 Northbound at Junction 3 at about 03:00 local time.
The five teenagers who died have been named locally as Joe Carthy from Athy, County Kildare, Alex McCarthy from Carlow, Kamil Pustkowski from Limerick, Jeremy O'Brien and Jack Kennedy, according to Irish broadcaster RTÉ News.
The injured family - two women aged in their 30s and one in her 20s, and the young boy - are understood to be from Carlow.
McManus said the teenagers had been in the car for a number of hours before the collision and gardaí had attempted to interact with them and bring the vehicle to a stop on "several occasions".
"At that stage our members would not continue in that pursuit and the directions that were given by our command and control centre were to disengage," she said.
"That would be the normal procedure for us that we do not engage with a car that has decided to take that sort of evasive action."
![Social Media A composite image of five young men. Some of them have taken selfies other are pictures that have been taken of them.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/news/480/cpsprodpb/c601/live/eddea4b0-9adc-11f1-a291-b542ee92de7c.jpg.webp) Social Media
"Our roads policing officers, whose speciality is obviously roads policing, do not have pursuit training," she said.
She added that officers could face serious personal consequences if they took action without the appropriate training.
The GRA, which supports rank and file police officers, would support tougher legislation, including harsher sentences and driving bans for people caught engaging in dangerous behaviour on the roads, she said.
McManus also described the aftermath of the crash as "horrific" for the officers who attended the scene.
McManus said gardaí who attended the scene could require counselling for "months or years" to deal with the psychological impact of what they witnessed.
![A satellite image of the east cost of Ireland. Outline on the image is the M9 road, as well as Junction 3 and Junction 4.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/news/480/cpsprodpb/72fc/live/124ff650-9a1f-11f1-aed2-8d6da8d75094.jpg.webp)
Pursuit training a 'critical shortfall'
Brendan O'Connor, a Donegal garda and a former president of the GRA, said he believed the public would be "shocked" at the lack of pursuit training.
"The GRA have raised this for many, many years," he told the BBC's Nolan Show, adding that it was a "pressing police issue" and the "terrible events in Kildare" expose a "critical shortfall" in capacity.
"There has been massive investment in An Garda Síochána, contrary to what's happening in Northern Ireland in relation to [police] funding, but police driver training has just seemed to be on the back foot and not prioritised," he claimed.
An Garda Síochána has been contacted for comment.
Road deaths in Ireland
Leo Lieghio, vice president of the Irish Road Victims Association, has called for greater urgency in tackling road deaths.
Lieghio's 16-year-old daughter, Marsia, was knocked down by a driver travelling at 50mph at a pedestrian crossing in Dublin in 2005. She died in hospital six days later.
He said the families of those killed and injured will be experiencing "torment".
"Their lives have been turned upside down through no fault of their own. They will be going through hell."
Lieghio added that there needs to be a stronger focus on consequences and early intervention, particularly for dangerous or criminal behaviour on the roads.
"We should be looking at structured intervention, something that teaches responsibility," he said.
Lieghio called for a "reform programme" aimed at young people involved in criminal activity on the roads, alongside greater responsibility from drivers and the wider public.
"We all have a responsibility on our roads, and if we see something wrong happening, we should be reporting it. We need consequences for a change of behaviour," he said.
Lieghio said each death has consequences that extend far beyond the person who loses their life.
"I can imagine what's going on in those hospitals now. I sat beside my daughter's bed for six days, praying and hoping for something to change, but she couldn't fight anymore," he said.
'Sadness, anger, compassion and grief'
The parish priest of Athy said his "heart, thoughts and prayers" are with all of those impacted by the "tragic situation".
Fr Seamus McEntee said he travelled along the same stretch of the motorway just hours before the crash took place.
He said the people he has spoken to feel "a mixture of emotions" and are "carrying sadness, anger, compassion and grief".
summary: Irish police were instructed to disengage from pursuing a car driving in the wrong direction on the M9 motorway in County Kildare before a fatal head-on crash. The collision resulted in the deaths of five teenagers and left several others, including a seven-year-old boy and three women, with serious or critical injuries. The Garda Representative Association stated that roads policing officers lack pursuit training and followed standard procedure by disengaging after the vehicle took evasive action.
key_points: Five teenagers were killed and four other people were seriously or critically injured in a head-on crash on the M9 in County Kildare.
Gardaí were ordered to disengage from pursuing the vehicle after it drove in the wrong direction and took evasive action.
The Garda Representative Association stated that roads policing officers do not have pursuit training.
The GRA and other safety advocates have highlighted a lack of driver training and called for stronger consequences and intervention for dangerous road behavior.

title: British couple on honeymoon killed in helicopter crash on Greek island of Sifnos
author: Sofia Ferreira Santos
content:
Plume of black smoke seen at site of deadly helicopter crash
- Published
A young British couple and their pilot were killed in a helicopter crash on the Greek island of Sifnos on Monday, Greek police have said.
They have been named as newlyweds Alexander Cromie and Marie Ebert, who were in Greece on their honeymoon.
The private helicopter crashed just metres from a landing pad, killing the pair and their pilot, a Greek national.
The couple are said to have taken the helicopter from the village of Markopoulo near Athens to the popular holiday island, Kathimerini reported.
Greece's aviation safety authority told the BBC it was investigating the crash and that its investigators were heading to the scene on Tuesday to gather evidence and speak to witnesses.
![Two-panel map of Greece showing the location of an approximate crash site near the island of Sifnos in the Aegean Sea. The upper panel locates Sifnos among the Cyclades islands southeast of Athens, with Athens and Markopoulo labelled. An inset map of Greece highlights the area shown. The lower panel is a satellite image of Sifnos, with a callout marking the âApproximate location of crashâ on the islandâs eastern coast. Scale bars indicate 20 km and 10 miles on the regional map, and 2 km and 1 mile on the satellite image.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1600/cpsprodpb/ddcc/live/164b52e0-9afb-11f1-aed2-8d6da8d75094.png)
The BBC has contacted the UK Foreign Office, the Greek authorities and the aviation company for comment.
Asset management firm Blackstone, where Cromie worked, said in a statement: "We are shocked by the tragic passing of three people including our colleague Alex Cromie and his wife Marie Ebert, who were celebrating their honeymoon.
"Alex was beloved by everyone who knew and worked with him at Blackstone, and our thoughts and prayers are with his loved ones."
A senior police official told the Times that the crash came just before the helicopter's scheduled landing time of 18:15 local time (16:15 GMT).
![A few people are seen working at a blackened site on a mountain](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/2048/cpsprodpb/2139/live/d5d51200-9acd-11f1-a291-b542ee92de7c.jpg)
Emergency services personnel and locals were pictured working at the crash site to extinguish flames
Sifnos' Deputy Mayor, Manolis Foundoulakis, arrived at the scene shortly after the incident and told local news site Newsit there was almost "nothing left" of the aircraft.
He said locals saw the helicopter crash within metres of their homes and had described a "bizarre engine noise coming from the aircraft" as it was about to land.
He said two of the victims were found in the wreckage, while the third was a short distance away.
Firefighters worked to tackle a blaze which broke out after the crash, and the flames had been extinguished by Monday evening.
summary: A newlywed British couple and their Greek pilot were killed when their private helicopter crashed on the Greek island of Sifnos during their honeymoon on Monday. The aircraft went down just metres from a landing pad near the island's eastern coast, sparking a fire that was extinguished by firefighters. Greece's aviation safety authority is investigating the incident to determine the cause of the crash.
key_points: Newlyweds Alexander Cromie and Marie Ebert died in the crash along with their pilot.
The helicopter crashed metres from a landing pad on Sifnos just before its scheduled landing time.
Locals reported hearing a bizarre engine noise from the aircraft prior to the crash.
Greece's aviation safety authority is investigating the incident.
